catalog_quote: Trinidad English Creole tends to be syllable-timed and not stress-timed; therefore, Trinidad English Creole often has full vowels where Standard English has the reduced form / ə /. Unlike in many varieties of English, where pitch and stress are closely linked ... there is no clear connection between pitch and stress in Caribbean English-lexicon Creoles. ... Solomon (1993 : 34 – 36) describes the most common stress patterns in Trinidad English Creole disyllables: (a) low-high with stressed first syllable, e.g. PÒlíce; DÌSpúte; (b) high-low with stressed first syllable, e.g. NÓStrìl; SHÓULdèr . Trisyllables might be (a) low-low-high with stressed first syllable, e.g. CÀLlàloó; TÒbàgó; (b) low-high-high with stressed first syllable: Òbéáh; CÀRpéntér; (c) low-high-high with stressed second syllable, e.g. nèwsPÁpér; òrCHÉStrá; (d) low-low-high-high, e.g. vènèzuélá or (e) low-high-high…

audit.recode_to: Positional, quantity-sensitive left-oriented stress (trochaic feet built right-to-left, final-syllable extrametricality, main stress on the leftmost heavy syllable, defaulting to initial in light disyllables: ˈpoːliːs, ˈkanal, ˈbaluːn, ˈmamagaɪ, kaˈɹaɪliː), with lexical exceptions inherited from English; drop the tone/pitch accent framing as the primary analysis (Gooden & Drayton 2017:423 via Meer et al. 2024: no lexically contrastive tone; prominence = lexical stress, cued mainly by pitch alignment, duration and vowel quality). If the catalog's category set has no weight-sensitive left type for an English-lexifier creole, at minimum change 'No positional stress rule stated' to cite Drayton 2013 / Ferreira & Heitmeier 2021:22-24 and flag the left-edge rule, pending a read of Drayton 2013 in full.

sources.quote: 'The status of lexical stress in the phonologies of Caribbean English Creoles has been subject to some controversy, with some researchers suggesting a tonal system with lexically contrastive tone [Sutcliffe 2003]. However, empirical production research indicates the existence of a lexical stress system not only in TrinE but also in TEC [Drayton 2013; Gooden & Drayton 2017; Ferreira & Heitmeier 2021]. Syllables have no lexically contrastive tone. Instead, prominence at the word level is achieved by lexical stress, with stressed and unstressed syllables differing in syllable duration and vowel q
sources.note: Open perception study summarising the production literature (lexical stress system in TEC, no contrastive tone, TEC initial vs TrinE final stress in police-type words) and citing Sutcliffe 2003 as the tonal counter-view; downloaded now. (Also not yet obtained, lower priority: Sutcliffe 2003 'Eastern Caribbean suprasegmental systems' in Aceto & Williams eds., VEAW G30, 265-296; Solomon 1993 pp.34-37 in full.)

sources.access_detail: a copy the project holds (available on request)
sources.quote: 'In parametric terms (Hayes 1995), TrinE exhibits patterns of formation of left-headed feet built from right to left. TrinE is a quantity-based system ... heavy syllables tend to attract and anchor stress ... highly ranked final syllable extrametricality ... Main stress in TrinE falls on the leftmost or only syllable in a word with heavy syllables' (karailee /kʌˈɹaɪliː/). 'Solomon (1993:37) claims ... an apparent shift towards the first syllable primary stress in monomorphemic disyllabic words, possibly under the influence of TrinEC rules' — TrinEC /ˈpoːliːs/, /ˈkanal/, /ˈbaluːn/, /ˈdjuːɹɛs/ '
sources.note: Open specialist description (co-author = Drayton) giving an explicit metrical analysis (left-headed feet R-to-L, quantity-sensitive, final extrametricality, leftmost-heavy main stress) and attributing initial stress in disyllables (POlice, CAnal, BAlloon) to TrinEC stress rules; downloaded now.

sources.citation: Drayton, Kathy-Ann. 2013. The prosodic structure of Trinidadian English Creole. PhD dissertation, Dept. of Modern Languages and Linguistics, University of the West Indies, St. Augustine. (UWISpace hdl 2139/45098: abstract page only.)
sources.access_detail: a copy the project holds (available on request); access check: open copy online
sources.quote: 'The thesis examines the organization of prominence relations within the syllable, word, and sentence ... The Prosodic Word is shown to encode prominence in the form of a left-edge stress, and through recursion, incorporate morphologically complex words. At higher levels ... the thesis argues for an Accentual Phrase as an intermediate category.'
sources.note: The only full-length phonological/instrumental study of TEC word and phrase prosody; its abstract states the Prosodic Word has 'left-edge stress', directly against our 'lexical, no positional rule' coding built on a survey retelling of Solomon 1993.

sources.citation: Meer, Philipp & Robert Fuchs. 2022 [online 2021]. The Trini Sing-Song: Sociophonetic variation in Trinidadian English prosody and differences to other varieties. Language and Speech 65(4), doi 10.1177/0023830921998404 (PMC9669731).
sources.access_detail: a copy the project holds (available on request)
sources.quote: Phrase-level F0 study (pitch level, range, dynamism) of standard TrinE; for TEC it relays Drayton 2013: intonation phrases structured into accentual phrases with L* pitch accents and H boundary tones, which Drayton (2013:260) holds responsible for the 'sing-song' impression. No statement on word-stress placement.
